title: reads the index once for --check, however many entries there are
why: --check would start a git for every entry again, which outgrew the unit suite's 30 s on a Windows runner (issue 670).

title: reads the index once to look at the entries before a run, then asks if the tree is clean
why: A run's look at every entry before it starts would start a git for each of them again.

title: refuses a file git does not track, untracked or ignored, and leaves it as it was
why: An untracked or ignored file, which nothing else holds a copy of, would be mutated, and its original lost if the restore failed.

title: refuses every entry, saying why, where git cannot list the files it tracks
why: A git that could not list the index would read as an index with nothing in it: every file called untracked, and what went wrong never said.

title: is read from the index at each call, so a file added between two calls is seen
why: A list of tracked files kept for the life of the process would call a file added since untracked, and one removed since tracked.

title: is refused for a path not written as git lists it: no "./", "//" or "/./", nothing after a last "/" but a name
why: A path such as src/a.ts/. would reach the file system as src/a.ts but git as no file at all, so an edit to it would be invisible to the dirty-tree checks.

find: new TextDecoder('utf-8', { fatal: true, ignoreBOM: true })
title: takes a name that is not UTF-8 for none, never for one spelled with U+FFFD, and keeps a leading U+FEFF
why: A tracked name that is not UTF-8 would be read as one spelled with U+FFFD, and an untracked file of that spelling would pass as tracked.

find: new TextDecoder('utf-8', { fatal: true, ignoreBOM: true })
title: takes a name that is not UTF-8 for none, never for one spelled with U+FFFD, and keeps a leading U+FEFF
why: A tracked name that begins with U+FEFF would lose it, and the untracked file named without it would pass as tracked.
